newsitem.title: CHINA: Top China leader urges state firms to issue shares.
newsitem.headline: Top China leader urges state firms to issue shares.

text.p: China's economist tsar Zhu Rongji has urged lumbering state enterprises to look to stock markets as a means to raise capital rather than relying on credit, state media said on Thursday.

In a lengthy speech published in all major state newspapers, Vice Premier Zhu said Beijing was determined to fulfil its target of dragging most state firms out of their cycle of losses within the next three years.
Speaking after a tour of major state-owned giants in the northeastern industrial province of Liaoning, Zhu gave a strong hint of Beijing's plans for future reforms of its loss-making state sector.
Chinese sources said the no-nonsense economic boss also told a group of large listed firms that going public was not a ticket to do as they pleased.

"I think Zhu came down to instil some reality in people to let them know that while they might think that now they are listed they can do what they like, they can't, they still have to listen to the boss, and the boss is Zhu Rongji," said one securities industry source.

Zhu's speech gave a taste of future direction and apparently delivered his blessing to China's surging stock markets that he has battled to regulate this year by citing their usefulness in reviving state firms.
Raising funds on the stock markets rather than reliance on state handouts appeared to be the way of the future, he said.

"Following the day by day regularisation and stabilisation of China's stock markets, the direct raising of capital through the stock markets can become a major source of capital for state-owned enterprises," Zhu was quoted as saying.

The government would encourage mergers among listed state firms and loss-making firms that had good prospects, he said, a move in line with Beijing's campaign to create large conglomerates that it hopes will wield a stronger competitive capacity in China's new sink-or-swim marketplace.
Such mergers could give a new start to state-owned firms and invigorate listed companies, Zhu said.

Zhu criticised state firms that want to expand in sectors where production is already at over capacity, seeking credit that they may not be able to repay and adding to the burden of state banks already laden with bad debt held by state firms.
Zhu stressed the necessity to tackle problems that for decades have prevented many of China's huge and unwieldy state firms from turning a profit, including poor management and surplus staffing.
"A major reason for the difficulties of state-owned enterprises is the excessive number of surplus workers," he was quoted as saying.
"Only by really cutting down the numbers of surplus workers, reducing costs and raising profits will enterprises have a hope of surviving and developing," Zhu warned.

Economists and analysts say that finding the courage to push ahead with unpalatable reforms of the flagging and long cosseted state sector will almost certainly be a major issue at a crucial five-yearly Communist Party congress in late September or early October.
Officials had said state enterprises would be a priority this year.

However, progress has been slow amid fears the state would lose its predominance and that bankruptcies and streamlining would result in mass unemployment and social unrest -- anathema to China's communist leadership.

China's leaders and economists are currently debating whether to break with four decades of socialist tradition by moving away from the sacred cow of the state sector as the dominant sector of China's economy and allowing private enterprise a larger role.

China's lumbering state sector has shown signs of improving its performance in the first half of this year after an unprecedented net loss in 1996, officials have said. They have declined to give details.
